title: Politics in India: Recent Developments in Indian Politics

learn.hook: Between 1989 and 1992, India saw a hung Parliament, a former Prime Minister assassinated, an economic crisis and the biggest caste and religious mobilisations in decades. The decade reshaped Indian politics.
points: In 1984, after Indira Gandhi's assassination, Rajiv Gandhi led the Congress to a massive victory. But in 1989 the Congress lost its majority, ending the era of Congress dominance often called the 'Congress system'.
Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated on 21 May 1991, during the election campaign, by members of the LTTE. After the election, P.V. Narasimha Rao became Prime Minister.

Key developments of the period: the defeat of the Congress in 1989 and the end of the Congress system; the Mandal issue (1990), which brought backward-caste politics to the centre; the New Economic Policy of 1991, which began economic reforms; and the Ayodhya movement, which culminated in the events of December 1992.
These developments led to multi-party competition at the national level. No single party could easily win a majority, and coalition governments became common.

example.q: List four developments of 1989-1992 that changed Indian politics.
steps: End of the Congress system after the 1989 election.
Mandal issue: OBC reservations in 1990.
New Economic Policy of 1991.
The Ayodhya movement and the events of December 1992 (and Rajiv Gandhi's assassination in 1991).
example.answer: End of Congress dominance; Mandal; economic reforms; Ayodhya

learn.reallife: Many of today's major regional parties, from Bihar to Tamil Nadu, became powerful national players in the coalition politics that began in this period.

topics.title: The era of coalitions: National Front and United Front

learn.hook: From December 1989 to March 1998, six different leaders served as Prime Minister. Parties that had fought each other in elections propped up governments from outside.
points: In the 1989 election, the Congress emerged as the largest party but was far short of a majority. The National Front, an alliance of the Janata Dal and some regional parties, formed the government under V.P. Singh.
The National Front government received support from two very different sides: the BJP and the Left Front, both from outside the government. It lasted less than a year, after the BJP withdrew support.
In 1996, after a short-lived BJP government, the United Front, a coalition of regional and other non-Congress, non-BJP parties, formed the government with Congress support from outside.
The United Front Prime Ministers were H.D. Deve Gowda (1996-97) and I.K. Gujral (1997-98).
These governments showed that coalitions could bring regional parties to the centre of national power, but also that outside support made governments unstable.

example.q: Why were the National Front and United Front governments unstable?
steps: They depended on support from parties outside the government.
The supporting parties had very different ideologies (the BJP and the Left in 1989; the Congress in 1996-98).
When outside support was withdrawn, the governments fell.
example.answer: They relied on outside support from parties with different ideologies

topics.title: NDA and UPA: coalitions become the norm

learn.hook: From 1989 to 2014, no single party won a Lok Sabha majority on its own. Governing meant building alliances.
points: In 1998 the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) formed the government under Atal Bihari Vajpayee. It lost a confidence vote in 1999, but returned to power after the 1999 election and ruled until 2004.

In 2004 the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) formed the government, with Manmohan Singh as Prime Minister. The UPA won again in 2009, and Manmohan Singh was Prime Minister from 2004 to 2014.
From 1989 to 2014, coalition and alliance governments were the norm at the Centre. Both national parties had to share power with state-level and regional parties.
Coalition politics made bargaining and accommodation central to government. Alliances were often formed on practical, pragmatic grounds rather than shared ideology.
Exercise tip: order the coalition governments by date, from the National Front to the UPA.

topics.title: The political rise of the Other Backward Classes: Mandal and after

learn.hook: In August 1990 a government decision on reservations sparked protests across north India and changed the shape of Indian politics for decades.
points: The Janata Party government set up the Second Backward Classes Commission in 1978 (announced in December 1978 and formally appointed on 1 January 1979), chaired by B.P. Mandal; it is known as the Mandal Commission. It submitted its report in 1980.

The Commission recommended reserving 27 per cent of seats in educational institutions and government jobs for the Other Backward Classes (OBCs). It also made other recommendations, such as land reform, to improve their conditions.

In August 1990, the National Front government under V.P. Singh decided to implement the recommendation of 27 per cent reservation for OBCs in central government jobs. This led to violent protests in many cities, especially by students opposed to the decision.

In the Indra Sawhney case (1992), the Supreme Court upheld OBC reservation, with conditions such as excluding the better-off sections (the 'creamy layer') and keeping overall reservations within limits.

Political fallout: OBC and Dalit-based parties grew. The Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), founded by Kanshi Ram in 1984, came to power in Uttar Pradesh in 1995. Other parties with strong OBC support also became powerful in north India.

steps: 1978: Mandal Commission set up by the Janata government.
1980: report recommends 27% reservation for OBCs.
1990: V.P. Singh government implements it in central jobs; protests follow.
1992: Supreme Court upholds it in the Indra Sawhney case.

learn.reallife: OBC reservation in central government jobs and in central universities and institutions like IITs and AIIMS today traces back to the Mandal Commission's recommendation.

topics.title: Ram Janmabhoomi movement, the 2019 verdict and the temple

learn.hook: One site in Ayodhya was at the centre of a legal and political debate for decades, until a unanimous Supreme Court verdict in 2019 settled the dispute.
points: The Ram Janmabhoomi movement sought the construction of a Ram temple at the site in Ayodhya believed by many Hindus to be the birthplace of Lord Ram. In 1986 a Faizabad district court ordered the opening of the locks of the structure at the site. The movement grew into a major national issue, and the BJP made it a central part of its politics.
In 1990, BJP leader L.K. Advani led a Rath Yatra from Somnath in Gujarat towards Ayodhya to build public support for the movement.

On 6 December 1992, the three-domed structure at the disputed site was demolished by people who had gathered there. This was followed by communal violence in several parts of the country, and some state governments were dismissed.

The dispute went through a long legal process. On 9 November 2019, a five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court gave a unanimous verdict: the disputed land was to be given to a trust for building a Ram temple, and five acres of land elsewhere in Ayodhya were to be given for a mosque.

The verdict was accepted peacefully across the country, showing the strength of the legal process in resolving disputes. Construction of the Ram temple at the site began in 2020, and its consecration (pran pratishtha) ceremony was held in January 2024.

example.answer: Disputed land to a trust for a Ram temple; five acres elsewhere for a mosque

learn.reallife: The peaceful acceptance of the 2019 verdict across India is often cited as an example of how courts can settle even the most sensitive disputes.

learn.hook: In 2014, for the first time since 1984, a single party won a majority in the Lok Sabha on its own. Yet many ideas that grew in the coalition era were shared across parties.
points: Lok Sabha elections from 2004 to 2019: the Congress-led UPA won in 2004 and 2009. In 2014 the BJP won a majority on its own (282 seats), the first time any party had done so since 1984, and it formed the government with its NDA allies under Narendra Modi. In 2019 the BJP won an even larger majority (303 seats). (In 2024 the BJP won 240 seats, short of a majority on its own, and the NDA formed the government with its allies, again under Narendra Modi.)
A growing consensus emerged among most parties on four points. First, agreement on the new economic policies: most parties support economic reforms, even if they differ on details.
Second, acceptance of the political and social claims of the backward castes: almost all parties support reservation for backward classes and seek their support.
Third, acceptance of the role of state-level parties in national governance: the line between regional and national parties has become less important.

Fourth, emphasis on pragmatic considerations rather than ideological positions: alliances are often made without full ideological agreement. Exercise tip: explain the political impact of Mandal and order the coalition governments by date.

example.q: Name the four elements of the new consensus in Indian politics.
steps: Agreement on new economic policies.

Pragmatism rather than ideology in forming alliances.
example.answer: Economic policy; backward-caste claims; role of state parties; pragmatism over ideology
